text.text: ure 1 sketches this design, and Figure 2 follows one simulated pair of agents through these phases.
Figure1: Conceptual overview.
Policies are first trained in a stable world, where patches never degrade.
In evaluation, each panel sketches the agent's landscape of beliefs, in which the ball represents the agent and the deep canals represent the agent's confident beliefs about the food's location.
During canalization, the familiar patches degrade with use, even as beliefs about them grow more precise.
At 300 s, two new patches appear far away.
CDR agents are then decanalized for 100 s: their beliefs flatten and their choices become more random, letting them reach the new patches.
CCC agents receive no intervention and are slow to find the new patches-and some never do.
The panel below shows how the homeostatic state h changes over time; ideally, it stays close to the setpoint of 0 (dotted line).
Both conditions fall into a deficit during canalization.
However, only CDR agents tend to return toward the setpoint during the intervention-CCC agents tend to stay far below it until late in recanalization.
Figure3: Evaluation protocol.
Policies are trained in a stable world, and their weights are then fixed.
Each evaluation trial runs in the changing world, where the familiar patches degrade with use from the start and two new patches appear at 300 s.
During canalization, the two conditions are identical, and the precision P c of the agent's beliefs grows as it observes and harvests.
During the intervention, CDR agents are decanalized with a dose d and a temperature boost b: every precision is multiplied by 1 -d, and the sampling temperature T is raised to 1 + bd.
CCC agents keep the baseline settings (d = 0, T = 1).
In recanalization, both return to baseline; beliefs, position, and h carry over.
The main setting is d = 1, b = 1; we also tested d = 0.5 and b = 0, 3, and 10, with b = 10 at full dose only (Section 2.7).
Outcomes are compared in recanalization (Table1).
Figure4: Homeostatic state in a sample trial (HRL; the paired trial of Figure2).
The two agents share a trajectory during canalization.
During canalization, h falls because the familiar patches degrade with use, which they did not do in training (in fact, without new patches, h would keep falling for most agents).
During the intervention (shaded), after the new patches appear, the CDR agent climbs close to the setpoint, while the CCC agent stays far below it.
In recanalization, the CDR agent stays near the setpoint, and the CCC agent recovers only after it finds a new patch, late in the phase.
Figure 5: CCC and CDR across phases for HRL (top) and NF (bottom).
Columns show mean absolute h, mean h, the fraction of trials trapped, and harvests from the two new patches.
Points are means across four training seeds, evaluated in 64 paired trials; bars show 95% t-intervals over training seeds.
Conditions coincide before the intervention.
After it, CDR agents of both types have lower mean absolute h and are trapped less often.
They harvest from the new patches sooner, but after the intervention, the two conditions harvest from them about equally.
the main measure, HRL agents gained far more.
Decanalization lowered their 464 MAE by 83 points, against 34 for NF agents, and the NF benefit shrank to-465 ward zero at higher boosts.
The difference held for every pair of HRL and NF 466 policies trained with the same seed.
This was not because NF agents failed 467 to escape.
Decanalization freed even more NF agents than HRL agents from 468 trapping (33 percentage points fewer trapped, against 23), and NF agents 469 also reached the new patches sooner.
The difference came afterward.
Figure6: Exploratory analysis of the two components of decanalization, for HRL agents at full dose.
Bars show mean absolute h (MAE) in the recanalization phase, averaged over the four trained policies, each evaluated on 64 trials.
The dashed line marks no intervention (CCC), so the benefit of each version is how far its bar falls below the line.
Below each label are the factors applied to every precision P c and the sampling temperature T during the intervention.
The darker bar is the main intervention.
Each version's difference from CCC and the corresponding NF results are in Appendix Table 5.
Not all CCC agents stayed trapped.
Many eventually found the new patches and, once there, harvested from them about as often as CDR agents did.
But they found them late, often after falling deep into deficit, and more than a third of HRL CCC agents never found them within the trial.
Decanalized agents reached the new patches sooner and spent far less time far from the setpoint.

The clinical parallel is that many people recover from entrenched patterns without intervention; it simply takes them longer, and the cost lies in the time spent far from where they need to be and the consequences of extreme deviations from the ideal.Both HRL and NF agents escaped their failing patches, but only the HRL agent is rewarded for staying near its setpoint once it does.
The NF agent's reward ignores everything above the setpoint, so nothing tells it to stop once it is full.
In the terms of our heating analogy, it is a heater that gets credit for warming a cold room but no penalty for overheating it.
Once freed, decanalized NF agents kept eating past the setpoint and ended far above it (mean h of +112), so their regulation improved much less than that of HRL agents.
Decanalization gave both agents a chance to reach better food, and what each did with that chance depended on what it was rewarded for.
This is the point ofKeramati and Gutkin's (2014) homeostatic account.
text.formatted: This is the point of<ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Keramati and Gutkin's (2014)</ref> homeostatic account.

text.text: An HRL agent is rewarded for moving toward its setpoint from either side, so for it, seeking reward and staying stable are the same thing.
For an NF agent, they can come apart-instability and even large deviations from the setpoint are common.
Decanalization worked on the agent's beliefs, which is where its canalization lived.
Lowering its confidence in what it believed about each cell let new evidence change its cognitive map more easily.
This relaxing of beliefs is the core of the REBUS account (Carhart-Harris & Friston, 2019).
text.formatted: This relaxing of beliefs is the core of the REBUS account (Carhart-Harris & Friston, 2019).

text.text: RE-BUS concerns high-level priors, such as beliefs about oneself and the world, while ours are low-level beliefs about where food is, so the parallel is one of mechanism rather than content.
